name: Fat repositioning (tear trough)
lead: Fat repositioning is a lower-eyelid surgical technique in which orbital fat that would otherwise bulge as an under-eye bag is mobilised and moved over the infraorbital rim to fill the hollow below it, known as the tear trough [1][2]. It contrasts with traditional lower blepharoplasty, in which herniated fat is simply removed.

The approach is reported in the plastic surgery literature through case series, including a 66-patient series of transconjunctival repositioning in the sub-orbicularis oculi fat (intra-SOOF) plane [2], a 97-patient cohort studying external fixation of the moved fat in transcutaneous surgery [3], and a 232-patient series asking whether visibly herniated fat is needed for the procedure to be performed [4]. Evidence is limited to such surgeon-reported series; the sources reviewed contain no randomised trial.

paras: In fat repositioning the orbital fat pads are released and redistributed along the infraorbital rim to smooth contour irregularities and treat tear trough deformity, rather than being excised [1]. It may be done through an incision inside the lower lid (transconjunctival) or just below the lashes (transcutaneous), and is often supplemented by procedures such as canthopexy or midface elevation to improve the transition from lower lid to cheek [1].

A 2006 case series described transconjunctival repositioning with dissection in the intra-SOOF plane in 66 consecutive patients with an average age of 56 [2]. A 2025 study of 97 patients examined percutaneous external fixation of the repositioned fat in transcutaneous surgery, noting that internal fixation had remained the standard in that approach while external fixation had gained popularity in transconjunctival surgery [3].

A 2024 series of 232 patients, including 34 who had previously had fat removed, evaluated the procedure in people with minimal or no excess fat herniation, challenging what the authors describe as a strong belief that herniated fat is a prerequisite [4]. A published discussion of that paper also exists [5].

Lower-eyelid surgery in general carries risks including eyelid malposition, which is why adjunct procedures such as canthopexy are used by some surgeons [1]. Procedure-specific complication rates are not summarised here because the available abstracts do not report them in full.

Published human studies are surgeon-reported case series: a 66-patient intra-SOOF series [2], a 97-patient external fixation cohort [3] and a 232-patient series on fat herniation [4]. No randomised controlled trials were found in the sources reviewed.

timeline.event: Case series of transconjunctival fat repositioning via the intra-SOOF plane published (66 patients) [2].
Series of 232 patients examines the procedure with minimal or no fat herniation [4].
Study of percutaneous external fixation of repositioned fat in transcutaneous surgery (97 patients) [3].

card.summary: Moving under-eye fat into the tear trough instead of cutting it out; documented in surgeon case series, not randomised trials.
card.note: Surgical procedure; evidence is retrospective case series.

quick.overview:
Fat repositioning is a lower-eyelid surgery that shifts the fat pads responsible for under-eye bags down over the bony rim to fill the tear trough hollow, instead of removing them.

Published evidence consists of surgeon-reported case series of 66, 97 and 232 patients. No randomised trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Orbital fat is released and redistributed over the infraorbital rim through an incision inside the lower lid or just under the lashes, sometimes secured with fixation sutures [1][3].
quick.risks: Lower-eyelid surgery can cause eyelid malposition and other complications; surgeons sometimes add a canthopexy to reduce that risk [1]. Procedure-specific complication data are not summarised in the sources reviewed.
